posts.content:
Anyone can build a robot that looks like a person. Building one that moves like a person—that makes contact with the world and keeps its balance when the floor drops away—is a much harder problem. And it's a hardware problem.
That's the throughline of a Science Magazine / American Association for the Advancement of Science paper from our co-founder and Chief Robot Officer, Jonathan Hurst, "Physical AI is enabled by mechanical hardware."

One line that stuck with us: "Looking back on some of today's humanoid robots with precise human dimensions or five-fingered hands will be akin to looking back at early heavier-than-air flying machine prototypes."

We didn't understand the physics of flight then; we're at that stage with locomanipulation now. The payoff, Jonathan argues, is a future full of human-centric machines with familiar features but clear differences.

We shared this when it published last week. It's now available to read in full, no paywall, on our site.

Read the full paper. Link in comments.

AI can make a robot smarter, but it can’t change the physics of the robot it’s running on.

That’s the argument our co-founder and Chief Robot Officer Jonathan Hurst makes in a new paper published today in Science Magazine: “Physical AI is enabled by mechanical hardware.”

As some predict that humanoid hardware will become a commodity and software will do the differentiating, Jonathan pushes back.

“AI is just software trapped behind the physics of the hardware it is running on.”

For robots to move, manipulate objects, and interact safely with people, intelligence still has to work through the physical dynamics of the machine itself.

The future of physical AI depends on getting the physical part right.

Congratulations to Jonathan on this important contribution to the field.

Read the full paper in Science Robotics. Link in comments.

posts.content:
I read this in Forbes this week, and it's more than worth the five minute read: Jeff Burnstein, who's spent four decades at the A3 - Association for Advancing Automation, was asked point blank whether humanoid robots are the future of factories or just another hype cycle. His answer: we're heavy in the hype cycle. And the only humanoid he's aware of that actually operated in a U.S. production facility is Agility Robotics' Digit, at a GXO Logistics plant. Digit is also on the floor at a Schaeffler manufacturing facility. We've logged more than 65,000 hours of operation.

I appreciated that call out but I'd add one more thing about the hype cycle...

Most demo videos aren't lying about what a robot can do...once. They're just not telling you about the hard part. Turning a demo into a safe, revenue-generating deployment is a completely different problem. We built Digit around solving for the hard part, not the demo. It doesn't always make for a great video. It does make for a great business.

Burnstein's own data backs this up in a way that gets missed constantly: robot sales and U.S. unemployment move in opposite directions, not the same one. The real threat was never automation; it's losing the ability to compete at all.
He's also right that safety, not intelligence or dexterity, is the actual bottleneck. No humanoid has shipped yet that can work safely outside a cage. Until that changes industry-wide, "scale" stays a slide in a pitch deck.

Burnstein pegs today's unfilled manufacturing jobs at 500,000 and projects that number to reach 1.9 million by 2033. That gap gets closed by whoever can actually deploy safely outside of a cage, not by whoever has the best demo.

Worth the read: https://lnkd.in/gr_p_eV8

posts.content:
Why put a roboticist on stage at an energy conference?

Because the labor shortage runs through all of it. Supply chains, construction velocity, and the skilled trades.

At the Energy Future Forum 2026 in May, our co-founder and board chairman Damion Shelton sat down with Mark P Mills to make the case: in US warehouses alone, roughly 1 million manual-labor jobs sit unfilled, work that needs a person, with no person to do it.

That's the gap Digit is built to close. Not science fiction, a real robot doing real work in a commercial warehouse today. And here's the distinction that matters: Digit takes on tasks, not jobs. It handles the repetitive work people don't want so they can move to safer, higher-skilled, better-paid roles.

Damion and Mark also get into what changed to make this possible, why we're not building robot butlers, and why keeping people safe matters more than how fast we scale.

posts.content:
Tuesday's decision by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to address the growing national and economic security risks posed by foreign-made advanced robotic devices, including humanoids, marks an important step toward addressing those concerns before they become deeply embedded across an entire industry, much like what happened in the drone market. By adding this new category to the FCC's Covered List, the Commission has taken an important step in that direction. This decision rewards companies that have invested in building trusted domestic supply chains from the ground up and ensures that humanoid robots like Digit, which is engineered and assembled here in the US, can be deployed safely, securely, and at scale.

At the same time, Agility's academic roots and continued commitment to innovation give us a deep appreciation for maintaining access to all of the tools and technologies that advance robotics research. Both of these goals can be accomplished, and we will continue to advocate for policies that simultaneously protect US security and privacy and enable continued US technology leadership.

At Agility, we have spent years moving beyond the lab into real-world commercial deployments, partnering with customers to understand and meet their security requirements and operational expectations. As the commercial market continues to mature, we look forward to contributing to the growing policy discussion in Washington and helping shape a framework that strengthens American leadership while fostering continued innovation.

Read the FCC's fact sheet: https://lnkd.in/guXpamhf

For additional details on our policy vision, read our recent white paper, Safeguarding America's Humanoid Future:  https://lnkd.in/g-HeHEuB
